item.title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
item.description: arXiv:2610.18924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine-learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open-source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor-based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder-spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of $\geq$ 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin-generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin-trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter-label-free training.
item.dc:creator: Alec H. Follmer

item.title: A basis-set-free reference for the exact exchange-energy density and functional development
item.description: arXiv:2610.19031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The exact local exchange-energy density, obtained from the Slater potential of the Hartree-Fock exchange hole, is a central ingredient of Becke's B05 and B13 functionals and of many other local hybrids. It is usually evaluated in a Gaussian basis, so the local quantity retains a pointwise basis-set incompleteness error. We describe here a basis-set-free numerical code that solves the Kohn-Sham problem on real-space grids for atoms, diatomics, and polyatomics, and returns the exact local exchange-energy density together with the density, its derivatives, the kinetic-energy density, and the reverse Becke-Roussel hole quantities. Reconstructed from the published record of Becke's non-public NUMOL code, AXEL reproduces numerical atomic references through krypton, scalar-relativistic uranium orbital energies, and Becke's diatomic spectroscopic constants. We then extend the original local-density numerical framework to generalized-gradient and hybrid functionals. Comparisons with the independent adaptive-multiwavelet code MRChem give sub-millihartree agreement for Hartree-Fock and PBE0. The same calculations agree with large Gaussian-basis references to a similar level of accuracy. Atom-centred eXact Electronic Limit (AXEL) is intended as both a basis-set-free numerical reference and a platform for exchange-hole-based density-functional development.
item.dc:creator: Alastair J. A. Price

item.title: Dual-Resonator Organic Microcavities for Triplet-Triplet Annihilation Upconversion
item.description: arXiv:2610.19209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solid-state triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion offers a compelling route to harvest sub-bandgap photons to increase the efficiency of photovoltaics, but low sensitizer doping required to suppress non-radiative aggregation quenching severely restricts light absorption. Here, we present a dual-resonator planar silver microcavity housing a thermally co-evaporated rubrene:palladium phthalocyanine (PdPC) active layer designed to simultaneously enhance triplet-sensitizer absorption and out-couple upconverted emission. By aligning a dispersive cavity mode with the PdPC absorption peak at $32^\circ$, we achieve a 12-fold enhancement in absorptance at 665 nm. This absorption boost, combined with directional outcoupling through a second cavity mode, outweighs cavity-induced reabsorption losses to yield a 22-fold peak and 4.5-fold integrated enhancement in detected upconversion emission. Overall, this work highlights the potential of microcavity integration to substantially enhance solid-state upconversion performance across low-intensity optoelectronic applications.
item.dc:creator: Robert H. Gordon, Rachel C. Kilbride, Michael Hutton, Jenny Clark, Robert D. J. Oliver

item.title: Combined Absorption and Emission Study of Air Species in NASA EAST
item.description: arXiv:2610.19346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A suite of tunable diode laser absorption spectroscopy (TDLAS) diagnostics targeting rovibrational states of nitric oxide (NO) in the mid-infrared (MIR) and electronic states of atomic oxygen (O) and nitrogen (N) in the near-IR (NIR) was combined with optical emission spectroscopy (OES) for overlapping wavelengths at the NASA Electric Arc Shock Tube (EAST) facility for three selected high-temperature air experiments. Absorption features were probed at rates up to 1 MHz to provide quantitative, time-resolved measurements of temperature and species number density profiles behind incident shocks, enabling comparisons to spatially-resolved emission measurements, with the two typically agreeing within their respective uncertainties. Inferred time-histories are further compared to incident shock simulations from two one-dimensional models - one leveraging the Park two-temperature rates and the other more recent rate values - as well as the Data Parallel Line Relaxation (DPLR) code. For the two low-velocity cases (3.81 and 3.98 km/s) in which NO is probed, inferred temperatures are typically well-captured by all three models, although the NO number densities show stronger variation, agreeing better for the model with updated NO formation and dissociation rates. Finally, one high-velocity case (7.03 km/s) demonstrates the simultaneous resolution of three O-atom and six N-atom electronic states, with all states showing a steady increase in number density over time - possibly due to shock trajectory effects. Together, this combined absorption and emission study demonstrates resolution of many states of nonequilibrium air species, while directly comparing ground- and excited-state populations via the combined diagnostic strategy.
item.dc:creator: Jesse W. Streicher, Efaine Chang, Dylan L. Drescher, Christopher L. Strand, Ronald K. Hanson, Andrea Fagnani, Augustin C. Tibere-Inglesse, Brett A. Cruden

item.title: Density and excess molar enthalpy of 2-butanol + glyme liquid mixtures. Application of the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models to 2-alkanol + linear ether systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.19805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Densities and excess molar volumes ($V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at (293.15 to 303.15) K and excess molar enthalpies ($H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K are reported for the 2-butanol + 2,5-dioxahexane, or + 2,5,8-trioxanonane, or + 2,5,8,11-tetraoxadodecane, or + 2,5,8,11,14-pentaoxapentadecane systems at 95 kPa. Densities were measured using a densitometer Anton Paar DSA 5000, and excess enthalpies by means of a micro-calorimeter Tian-Calvet. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ data are positive, indicating that interactions between like molecules are dominant and that the main contribution to $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ is the interactional one. Our enthalpic data together with data from the literature have been used to evaluate the enthalpy of alcohol-glyme interactions, which are ranged between ($-$31 and $-$22) kJ mol$^{-1}$. From the comparison with $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results for glyme + heptane systems, and from the position of the investigated mixtures in the diagram $G_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ (excess molar Gibbs energy) vs. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$, it is shown that interactions are of dispersive type. 2-Alkanol + dipropyl ether (DPE), or + glyme systems have also been studied using the DISQUAC, UNIFAC (Dortmund) and ERAS models. According to ERAS results, physical interactions in glyme systems are dominant, while association effects are predominant in mixtures with DPE. The DISQUAC interaction parameters suggest that interactions related to the OH/O contacts are essentially dispersive. UNIFAC fails when representing thermodynamic properties of the studied solutions.
item.dc:creator: Fatemeh Pazoki, Jo\~{a}o Victor Alves-Laurentino, Susana Villa, Daniel Lozano-Mart\'in, Fernando Hevia, Luis Felipe Sanz, Juan Antonio Gonz\'alez

item.title: High-Harmonic Generation Probes Quantum Nuclear Fluctuations in Liquid Water
item.description: arXiv:2610.19967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nuclear quantum effects are essential for an accurate description of the hydrogen-bonded structure of liquid water, yet their spectroscopic signatures can be subtle and difficult to measure. Moreover, probing these effects in solution on femtosecond timescales (or below) is an open challenge that is pivotal for optical control of hydrogen bonds and ultrafast spectroscopy of proton transfer. Here, we combine path-integral molecular dynamics with real-time time-dependent density-functional theory to explore high-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid water from first principles, rigorously accounting for quantum nuclear delocalisation. Relative to classical-nuclei simulations, quantum sampling suppresses the harmonic yield around certain harmonics by up to an order of magnitude, inducing local structural minima. By analysing the ab initio simulations and reproducing the key effects with a simplified model Hamiltonian, we trace the physical origins of the interference minima to the broadening of valence-band states induced by hydrogen-bond fluctuations, a mechanism expected to generalise to other hydrogen-bonded structures. Our work shows that nuclear quantum effects are indispensable for capturing ultrafast electronic dynamics in liquids, and demonstrates the power of liquid HHG spectroscopy for attosecond probing of nuclear fluctuations.
item.dc:creator: George Trenins, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean, Angana Mondal, Angel Rubio, Hans Jakob W\"orner, Aaron Kelly, Ofer Neufeld, Mariana Rossi

item.title: Cartesian and Curvilinear Anharmonic Frequencies and Intensities: Perturb-then-Diagonalize Polyad Transport and Adiabatic Discrete-Variable Representation
item.description: arXiv:2610.20488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anharmonic intensities reveal vibrational coupling that band positions alone cannot determine. We derive explicit second-order infrared transition moments in curvilinear normal coordinates, including kinetic metric derivatives and transport through variational resonance polyads. The vibrational perturbation-to-second-order-then-diagonalization (VP2TD) treatment covers fundamentals, overtones, three-quantum transitions, and hot bands. A general computational platform combines Extended Symmetry-Adapted Local Coordinates (ESALCs), using Cartesian (ESALC-C) or internal (ESALC-I) primitives, with interchangeable quantum-chemical programs and parallel finite differences. Independent oscillator matrices verify the intensity equations; a molecular water check reproduces second-order amplitudes within $8.4\times10^{-8}$ atomic units. Comparisons with established tools reproduce a formaldehyde Fermi polyad within 0.163 cm$^{-1}$ and 0.061 km mol$^{-1}$ and water Raman activities within $10^{-7}$ Angstrom$^6$. For 29 matched formaldehyde rotational line pairs, the predicted hot-to-fundamental intensity ratio, using the measured lower-state energy, is consistent with the nuclear-spin-corrected median: the differences are 3.9% (ESALC-I) and 3.8% (ESALC-C), compared with a 15% uncertainty estimate for individual measured line intensities. Common analytic reference derivatives ensure identical harmonic observables, while internal coordinates reduce and localize intermode anharmonic couplings. Rotation-vibration constants extend the same tensor treatment. An integrated adiabatic discrete-variable representation treats large-amplitude motions, and finite-level partition functions provide anharmonic thermochemistry.
item.dc:creator: Vincenzo Barone

item.title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ans\"atze
item.description: arXiv:2610.19109v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant R\'enyi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ans\"atze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.
item.dc:creator: Prince Frederick Kwao, Bharath Sambasivam, Jason Saroni, Srivathsan Poyyapakkam Sundar, Edwin Barnes, Ayush Asthana

item.title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.19123v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Lawrence, Bodhi P. Vani, Ji Won Park, Natasa Tagasovska, Samuel Don Stanton, Andrew Martin Watkins, Michael Maser, Ewa M. Nowara

item.title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.19404v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Hongrui Sheng, Shutian Liang, Reid A. Coyle, Shyam Chand Pal, Peter Walther, Bin Feng, Xinyu Ding, Zhiling Zheng

item.title: Near-field contributions to cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer
item.description: arXiv:2610.20130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedding materials in optical cavities has emerged as a powerful strategy for controlling their physical properties. In this context, increasing attention has been devoted to the thermal Purcell effect, which describes how the radiative heat transfer between a material and its photonic environ- ment can be modified by the electromagnetic boundary conditions imposed by the cavity. Here, we investigate near-field effects in cavity-mediated radiative heat transfer in planar cavities composed of realistic, dissipative gold mirrors, extending previous work that considered ideal mirrors. We iden- tify the conditions under which near-field effects lead to a substantial enhancement of heat transfer between the material and a photonic thermal bath relative to free space, owing to the strong modi- fication of the photonic local density of states by evanescent modes within the cavity. In particular, we find that radiative heat flow can be enhanced by several orders of magnitude in cavities ranging from nanometer to micrometer scales, depending on the absorber frequency and dipole orientation. These findings suggest that near-field effects may be relevant to polariton chemistry experiments and other systems operating within this cavity length-scale regime. Our results add to the idea that cavities can modify material properties not only by engineering vacuum fluctuations in the strong light-matter coupling regime, but also by controlling radiative dissipation and heat transfer.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Mastropasqua, Martin Eckstein, Daniele Fausti, Francesca Fassioli

item.title: VEDA: Generation of 3D Molecules via Variance-Exploding Diffusion with Annealing
item.description: arXiv:2511.09568v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion models show promise for 3D molecular generation, but face a fundamental trade-off between sampling efficiency and conformational accuracy. While flow-based models are fast, they often produce geometrically inaccurate structures, as they have difficulty capturing the multimodal distributions of molecular conformations. In contrast, denoising diffusion models are more accurate but suffer from slow sampling, a limitation attributed to sub-optimal integration between diffusion dynamics and SE(3)-equivariant architectures. To address this, we propose VEDA, a unified SE(3)-equivariant framework that combines variance-exploding diffusion with annealing to efficiently generate conformationally accurate 3D molecular structures. Specifically, our key technical contributions include: (1) a VE schedule that enables noise injection functionally analogous to simulated annealing, improving 3D accuracy and reducing relaxation energy; (2) a novel preconditioning scheme that reconciles the coordinate-predicting nature of SE(3)-equivariant networks with a residual-based diffusion objective, and (3) a new arcsin-based scheduler that concentrates sampling in critical intervals of the logarithmic signal-to-noise ratio. On the QM9 and GEOM-DRUGS datasets, VEDA matches the sampling efficiency of flow-based models, achieving state-of-the-art valency stability and validity with only 100 sampling steps. More importantly, VEDA's generated structures are remarkably stable, as measured by their relaxation energy during GFN2-xTB optimization. The median energy change is only 1.72 kcal/mol, significantly lower than the 32.3 kcal/mol from its architectural baseline, SemlaFlow. Our framework demonstrates that principled integration of VE diffusion with SE(3)-equivariant architectures can achieve both high chemical accuracy and computational efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Peining Zhang, Jinbo Bi, Minghu Song

item.title: $GW$ reduced density matrix from iterated linearized Dyson equation
item.description: arXiv:2607.15695v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Iterating the Dyson equation with the static part of the self-energy leads to a concise and possibly improved expression of the one-body reduced density matrix from any self-energy approximation. Here we apply the procedure to Hedin's $GW$ approximation. The non-iterated $GW$ based density matrix was already known to yield accurate density matrices for molecular systems. We show that the Dyson-equation-based procedure is equivalent to the so-called variational Z-vector approach applied to the Random-Phase approximation energy functional, but only in the case of a Hartree-Fock mean-field starting point. When a generalized Kohn-Sham scheme is employed instead, the two approaches differ. By comparing the density matrix for a benchmark set of 34 small molecules to coupled-cluster reference values, we conclude that the iterated Dyson equation indeed produces improved density matrices for molecular systems. Interestingly, we observe that the excitation rank of the reference coupled-cluster matters much and that the inclusion of triple excitations (CCSDT) quantitatively changes the conclusions of the benchmark as compared to single and double excitations coupled-cluster (CCSD).
item.dc:creator: Fabien Bruneval, Erik Verzijl, Arno F\"orster, Mauricio Rodriguez-Mayorga

item.title: A Parameter-Free Reference Hamiltonian for Tight-Binding Vanadium Oxides
item.description: arXiv:2610.17687v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Density-functional tight binding has yet to yield a transferable description of vanadium oxides; for the standard second-order construction and the tested cells, we demonstrate that two of its approximations deviate by electron volts and offset each other in the band-index centroid separation between the V 3d and O 2p bands: the neutral two-centre reference omits electron-volt environmental terms, whereas the Mulliken charge model assigns the compact V 3d shell less than half of the self-consistent potential shift observed in PBE. Instead, we build a tight-binding model where the reference Hamiltonian derives from superposed neutral atoms, the full PBE exchange-correlation potential and frozen-core orthogonality, without adjustable terms, and where the orbital-resolved charge response employs three screening factors obtained from PBE linear response and an unscreened Coulomb range. Relative to the primary PAW reference, the plane-wave Harris-Foulkes energy differences of VO2 are matched by the reference energy at fixed geometry and the stated numerical settings, with signed deviations of +2.6 meV/atom for M1 relative to rutile (an energy difference of 92 meV/atom) and +6.2 and -5.2 meV/atom under 3% volume compression and expansion; the charge response reproduces 14 of 22 fitted and 5 of 8 held-out matched PBE responses within one tolerance, and 28 of the 30 within twice the tolerance, and in rutile the fitted first-radial V 3d shift is -4.39 eV, 0.47 eV more negative than PBE's -3.92 eV, whereas the tested DFTB2 charge model gives -1.53 eV. The convexity of the spinless model at fixed geometry prevents it from spontaneously differentiating symmetry-equivalent sites under the symmetries respected by its implemented operators and sampling, so within this model such differentiation in the Magn\'eli phases must arise from electron-lattice coupling or an explicit spin or correlation term.
item.dc:creator: Jun-qiang Lu

item.title: Does Pretraining Teach Chemical Language Models Chemistry?
item.description: arXiv:2610.18651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are pretrained on large corpora of molecules with the aim of learning representations that transfer to diverse downstream tasks. Here, we systematically study the effects of pretraining using a series of such CLMs across 64 molecular property prediction datasets. We find that the downstream gains of pretraining in CLMs do not scale and performance saturates below gradient-boosting baselines. Across the regimes evaluated, only supervised pretraining on traditional physico-chemical descriptors consistently improves downstream performance for the CLMs tested whereas some forms of pretraining result in models worse than a randomly initialized encoder. While models can resolve molecular structure well, they do so no better than a randomly initialized model, suggesting that, at best, CLMs learn descriptor-like properties in addition to low-level token statistics during pretraining, but surprisingly little chemistry beyond what classical molecular features already capture.
item.dc:creator: Leif Sieben, Yoel Zimmermann
